items.title: Will the Hubble “constant” ever become an actual constant?
items.summary: It was nearly a full century ago that enough data came in to map out both the distance to a significant number of extragalactic objects and also measure the amount that their light was redshifted: interpreted as an apparent recession speed away from us. When the distance and recession velocity of those objects were plotted against one another, an intriguing relationship emerged: the farther away we looked, the faster an object seemed to be moving away from us. Twice as far meant twice as fast; ten times as far meant ten times as fast. This linear relationship became known as Hubble’s Law (or more recently, the Hubble-Lemaître Law, since Georges Lemaître derived it first), with the slope of that line known as the Hubble constant. However, it turns out that this is a complete misnomer: not only does the expansion rate of the Universe change with time, but it isn’t even constant across all of space right at this very moment. In other words, there’s nothing constant about the Hubble “constant” at all! The variation of the expansion rate with time was predicted from the star, but the variation in space came as a surprise: only with the discovery of dark energy did we realize this was the case. And yet, dark energy may turn out to be the Hubble constant’s ultimate savior, as if it truly is a cosmological constant, then one day, the Hubble parameter will, far into the future, actually become a constant after all. Here’s the science of what’s really going on. Hubble’s discovery of a Cepheid variable in the Andromeda galaxy, M31, opened up the Universe to us, giving us the observational evidence we needed for galaxies beyond the Milky Way and leading us, in short order, to the discovery of the expanding Universe. Credits : NASA, ESA and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA); Illustration via NASA, ESA, and Z. Levay (STScI) Observationally, the story is seemingly straightforward. Beginning in the 1920s, our telescope technology became advanced enough — with large-enough aperture telescopes and the development of photographic plates — that we could start to resolve and identify individual stars in objects (i.e., galaxies) that were outside of our own Milky Way. The first such star was identified by Edwin Hubble in 1923: a Cepheid variable star, or a special class of star where, if you could measure the amount of time it took to brighten to its maximum, fainten to a minimum, and re-brighten back to its maximum again, you could know how intrinsically bright it was. Then, you could compare the observed brightness of that star (which you measured) with the intrinsic brightness that you just figured out, and that allows you to figure out the distance to it: the same way that, if you had a light bulb or candle with a known intrinsic brightness, then seeing how bright it appears would allow you to figure out how far away it is. This method for figuring out a distance in astronomy — the standard candle method — has since been extended to far more classes of objects than just Cepheid variable stars, and is one of the most useful tools in an observational astronomer’s arsenal. As was first noted by Vesto Slipher back in the 1910s, some of the objects we observe show the spectral signatures of absorption or emission of particular atoms, ions, or molecules, but with a systematic shift toward either the red or blue end of the light spectrum. When combined with distance measurements for those objects, this data gave rise to the initial idea of the expanding Universe: the farther away a galaxy is, the greater its light will appear redshifted to our eyes and instruments. Credit : Vesto Slipher, 1917, Proc. Amer. Phil. Soc. Then, in addition to figuring out the distance to that object, you can measure the light coming from that object as well. Rather than simply accumulating all the light of all different wavelengths together (a bolometric measurement ), or even by measuring the light across a variety of differently colored filters (a photometric measurement ), you could break that light up into all of its different component wavelengths, and measure the amount of light emitted at each specific wavelength along the way: a spectroscopic measurement . This technique, of spectroscopy, was the other key ingredient to uncovering the expanding Universe, and in turn, Hubble’s Law. When you break light up into its component wavelengths, you get to see an enormous number of features about it, including lines of two varieties: dark lines, known as absorption features, that occur at specific wavelengths and with specific intensities depending on the amount and density of any species of molecule, atom, or ion present, and bright lines, known as emission features, that occur at those same specific wavelengths that emerge from electrons transitioning between an excited state and a lower-energy state in molecules, atoms, or ions, at those same specific wavelengths. By comparing the observed wavelengths of (usually) absorption or (sometimes) emission features, we can determine an object’s redshift, and calculate the equivalent recession speed that corresponds to that redshift. Edwin Hubble’s original plot of galaxy distances, from 1929, versus redshift (left), establishing the expanding Universe, versus a more modern counterpart from approximately 70 years later (right). Many different classes of objects and measurements are used to determine the relationship between distance to an object and its apparent speed of recession that we infer from its light’s relative redshift with respect to us. As you can see, from the very nearby Universe (lower left) to distant locations over a billion light-years away (upper right), this very consistent redshift-distance relation continues to hold. Earlier versions of Hubble’s graph were composed by Georges Lemaître (1927) and Howard Robertson (1928), using Hubble’s preliminary data. Credit : E. Hubble; R. Kirshner, PNAS, 2004 Then, by plotting distance and redshift for the same sets of objects, together, we can make a graph for all sorts of extragalactic objects. This was done first by Georges Lemaître in an obscure 1927 paper (using much of Edwin Hubble’s data), then by Howard Robertson, independently, in 1928, and finally — and much more comprehensively — by Edwin Hubble himself in 1929. Although the points didn’t all lie exactly on a straight line, the overall trend was clear: the farther away an object was from us, on average, the greater its observed redshift, and hence, the greater its inferred recession velocity was. In all the time since those early measurements from the 1920s, throughout the early, mid, and late 20th century and even into the 1990s, we extended those measurements of distance and redshift to larger numbers of objects and evermore distant objects. Still, the slope of that best-fit line remained constant, and was named the Hubble constant. (In fact, the famed Hubble Space Telescope got its name because its primary mission was to pin down the measurement of that constant: the expansion rate of the Universe today.) Starting in the late 1990s, however, astronomers and astrophysicists made a shocking discovery. At the greatest of distances, the observed redshift-distance relation no longer followed a straight line, but instead departed from it. The theoretical implications of this — interpreted as evidence for the existence of dark energy — were astounding. This graph shows the 1550 supernovae that are a part of the Pantheon+ analysis, plotted as a function of magnitude versus redshift. The supernova data, for many decades now (ever since 1998), has pointed toward a Universe that expands in a particular fashion that requires something beyond matter, radiation, and/or spatial curvature: a new form of energy that drives the expansion, known as dark energy. items.title: You’re a Christian and a Buddhist (whether you like it or not)
items.summary: I’m going to call you a Christian. I don’t care if you don’t believe in God, or read the Bible, or accept that Jesus died for your sins. I’m going to call you a Christian anyway, because you do Christian things. You’re kind to others, you give to charity, you look after your neighbor. You don’t work on the Sabbath, you give gifts at Christmas, and you are awestruck by the sight of a cathedral touching the sunset sky. You’re a Christian. In this week’s Mini Philosophy interview , I spoke with the popular YouTuber and scholar of religion Andrew Henry. He introduced me to the term “orthopraxy,” which says being religious is not defined by what you believe but by what you do. If you behave according to a certain religion, you are that religion. To those born into a mostly Protestant culture, that might sound weird. In the West, we tend to treat religion as a matter of belief. But that idea is surprisingly local. The academic study of religion, Henry notes, “was mostly invented by Protestant scholars back in the late 1800s and 1900s,” and they built the category in their own image. Step outside it and you find that for most of history, and for much of the world today, religion was never mainly about what you believed. The ancient debate still with us If you think debates about religion are the worst, well, be prepared to be upset, because there’s a debate about even the word religion . The Roman philosopher Cicero argued that the word religion derives from relegere , “to re-read, go over again.” And so, the religiosi were people who carefully attended to every detail of a text, with the diligence of ritual. But around the year 300, the Christian writer Lactantius rejected Cicero’s idea and said religion comes from religare , “to bind,” because we are bound to God. Or, outside of the Christian mindset, we are bound to a creed, a dogma, a belief system. It’s an ancient debate we’re still having. The orthoprax follow in a line from Cicero — a religion is defined by what we do. The rituals we perform, the words we repeat, the small, everyday superstitions we find ourselves doing all define our religion. The orthodox follow from Lactantius and argue that religion requires assent to a belief. “I believe in one God, the Father almighty, maker of heaven and earth, of all things visible and invisible.” So who is right? Well, in terms of philosophy and theology, it depends on who you listen to or who you read. But in terms of how most of the world actually practices, things lean toward orthopraxy. In Confucianism and traditional Chinese beliefs, ancestor worship is far more important than any formal creed. In Japan, there is a saying: “born Shinto, marry Christian, die Buddhist.” A lot of Japanese people claim they aren’t religious, and yet pack out shrines at New Year’s, and Christian-style chapel weddings have been hugely popular since the 1990s, often led by a hired “priest” who isn’t ordained and quite possibly has never read the entirety of the Gospels. There’s an old joke within the Jewish community. Two people, Goldberg and Schwartz, are going to the synagogue. Goldberg goes to talk to God, while Schwartz goes to talk with Goldberg. The social, bonding aspect of Judaism is seen as an essential — even defining — part of the religion. Even within the Christian tradition, things aren’t so obvious. In 2012, the Richard Dawkins Foundation commissioned a poll of people who had ticked “Christian” on the 2011 census and found that only about 30% actually believed in Christianity’s teachings. Three out of four said it was because they had been baptized. Sixty percent hadn’t freely chosen to read any part of the Bible. If nothing else, it shows that “being religious” is complicated. The Buddhist who likes a walk Henry is orthoprax, but it turns out I’m more of an “essentialist,” or orthodox. I never even knew I was. And so I put it to Henry: “If I say I’m going for a walk and therefore I’m meditating, therefore I’m now a Buddhist, that’s not true, is it? By that logic I’m also a Hindu, a mystical Christian and a Sufi, which are incompatible.” Henry disagrees. In religious studies, he explained, there’s a long-running fight between “essentialists,” who often align with orthodoxy, and “functionalists,” who often align with orthopraxy. Essentialists think a religion has core ingredients, such as belief in the supernatural or membership in the right community, and without them it isn’t the real thing. Functionalists, like Henry, care less about what a practice is and more about what it does. Take, for example, the Nicene Creed. Every Sunday, millions of Christians recite it together. But millions of people also pack into stadiums and chant “USA! USA!” Both are rituals. Both produce the same feeling: we’re all in this together. So, for Henry, “slapping the label religion on either one of those is kind of artificial.” As for my incompatible-beliefs objection, Henry’s reply was to say that “people aren’t consistent.” He pointed to surveys suggesting that something like one in ten American evangelicals believe in reincarnation, which is “literal heresy” in a religion built on resurrection. And in the late Roman world, Christians “might go light some incense to Apollo at his temple on Tuesday and then go to the basilica and take the Eucharist on Sunday.” So if we think that beliefs are incompatible, Henry asks: according to whom? Usually, the answer is a religious authority. Catholics and Protestants disagree about what sits at the heart of Christianity. Sunnis and Shias disagree about Islam. Mormons insist they’re Christians, and a lot of other Christians say they’re not. There is good and bad news for my opening gambit. The good news is that orthopraxy says I might be right — how you behave is more important than what you believe. But the bad news is that if there’s no core, no central, absolute arbiter of “religious,” then nobody gets to hand out the labels: not the Pope, not the scholar, and certainly not me. You might be a Christian, but it’s not because I said so. This article You’re a Christian and a Buddhist (whether you like it or not) is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Immigration Is a Poorly Oiled Machine
items.summary: W hat would the U.S. immigration system look like if it were a machine, made of wheels and gears, controlled by belts and joints? In Kelly Lytle Hernández’s new book, Racist by Design: Two Centuries of U.S. Immigration Control , illustrations by the artist Mariah Tso help readers visualize such a contraption. Its parts are etched with important names and dates, Supreme Court cases, racist proclamations, and key concepts such as eugenics, no due process, and warrantless arrests. These sketches leave the impression that immigration control functions smoothly to exclude certain people—requiring only the occasional application of oil or glue. I would depict this machine differently, as would many historians. Its parts would be misaligned and mismatched; it would leak and spew smoke, expand and contract at random, and periodically grind to a halt. Yet Tso’s illustrations perfectly reflect the argument made by Lytle Hernández, a history professor at UCLA whose previous books have focused on the Border Patrol , mass incarceration , and Mexican anarchists . In Racist by Design , she contends that the United States since its founding has had a “whites-only immigration system.” That system has evolved, she says, but it remains “racist by design: It always has been and it still is.” We shouldn’t take “whites-only” literally, Lytle Hernández cautions. Instead, she writes, the term is an “interpretive device” to help us understand “racialized power.” She borrows language from the book Let This Radicalize You , in which two organizers, Kelly Hayes and Mariame Kaba, argue for studying a machine to figure out “what blows could actually disable it.” Lytle Hernández wants Racist by Design to land as a blow propelled by the force of history, inspiring collective action that will “keep pushing” the machine “and make it tip.” [ Read: What Stephen Miller gets wrong about human nature ] It isn’t controversial to say that racism has often motivated American immigration policy. Stephen Miller , Trump’s senior aide and homeland-security adviser, is hardly the first nativist to set federal priorities. Yet Lytle Hernández’s contention that more than two centuries of immigration control boil down to a story of white supremacy is an overstatement, even if it’s an important provocation. Lytle Hernández briefly acknowledges that “whiteness” isn’t always a simple category—that eugenicists have invented hierarchies among white people, and that racially neutral language, such as the word pauper , has been used to deport Irish people. But she doesn’t discuss how the meaning of whiteness changed over time; some white people were considered less white than others. She mentions other factors in debates over who can enter the country—sexuality, religion, public health, international diplomacy, ideology—but brushes them aside quickly so that they don’t muddy her point. These omissions and elisions make her argument vulnerable to challenges not only from historians who have studied other modes of discrimination, but also from political opponents eager to sabotage her cause. P lenty of evidence supports Lytle Hernández’s larger case. The Naturalization Act of 1790 said that only “a free white person” could naturalize, after living in the United States for two years. The first federal immigration ban was the 1803 Immigration Act, whose main proponents were enslavers seeking to block the entry of Black Caribbeans fleeing the Haitian Revolution. This pattern persisted for the next 150 years. In the mid-19th century, California state legislators levied a tax on foreign miners to keep nonwhite immigrants away from the gold mines. In 1882, Congress passed the Chinese Exclusion Act , which survived in different guises and iterations until 1943. And the 1924 Johnson-Reed Act established national-origins quotas that capped the total number of immigrants at 150,000 a year, while reserving 96 percent of those slots for European immigrants and 84 percent for those from northwestern Europe, according to Lytle Hernández. Senator David Reed, a Republican from Pennsylvania who co-authored the law, said, “We have closed the doors just in time to prevent our nordic population being overrun by lower races.” By 1940, Lytle Hernández writes, Europeans and Canadians, who at this point were all considered equally white, accounted for 94 percent of the foreign-born population living in the United States. Even after laws were liberalized and these numbers changed, members of both political parties tried to boost the proportion of white immigrants by prioritizing what the liberal Senator Ted Kennedy called the “old seed sources of our heritage.” This was all before the Trump administration made race-based immigration de facto American policy—most pointedly by deporting mainly nonwhite immigrants while welcoming white South Africans who claimed to be victims of a Black-led government. The author shows how the intrinsic racism of these moves is not accidental or incidental, but by design. She adds fresh insights as well by tracking the gradual concentration of immigration enforcement in the hands of the federal government, and by showing how fights over naturalization were entwined with debates over the treatment of Black people and Native Americans. And she reframes the immigration story as focusing on not only the people we let into the country, but also those we keep out. This complicates Americans’ conception of themselves as a nation of immigrants; we are also a nation that has excluded them. [ Read: Republicans vs. the Fourteenth Amendment ] Lytle Hernández is too good a historian to skip over more permissive periods, even when they fail to serve her argument. She calls the passage of the 1866 Civil Rights Act and the Fourteenth Amendment the “single-largest mass naturalization action in U.S. history,” because these laws “created more than four million new African American citizens.” When white settlers in the western U.S. challenged the birthright citizenship of Chinese Americans, the Supreme Court, in its 1898 ruling United States v. Wong Kim Ark , “unambiguously affirmed” that almost all children born in the United States were citizens. (The children of Native Americans, diplomats, and occupying troops in a hypothetical invasion were exceptions.) Nobody has conclusively counted the number of Americans born to undocumented immigrants who became citizens because of the Fourteenth Amendment, but the Pew Research Center has calculated that it has exceeded 100,000 a year since at least 1990. This past summer, in its Trump v. Barbara decision , the Supreme Court invalidated the president’s executive order limiting birthright citizenship and explicitly upheld the ruling in Wong Kim Ark . Trump’s solicitor general, D. John Sauer, argued that the authors of the Fourteenth Amendment intended to extend birthright citizenship only to freed slaves and their children. But a majority of the justices found that the language of the amendment was plain and applied to almost every person born in the United States, no matter their race or heritage. As alarming as it was that three justices sided with Trump, the decision, like earlier rulings from the top court, undermines Lytle Hernández’s idea of a whites-only immigration regime. Often, the author downplays government action by the courts, Congress, or presidents that benefited nonwhite immigrants. As a result of the 1965 Immigration and Nationality Act , which ended national-origins quotas, the United States went from being 16 percent nonwhite to 40 percent nonwhite in 60 years. Lytle Hernández frames this accomplishment as the unintentional result of mistaken reassurances; President Lyndon B. Johnson, for one, announced that it was not “a revolutionary bill,” and would not change people’s daily lives. items.title: A Luxury Apartment in Manhattan Is No Safer Than a Kitchen in East Oakland
items.summary: “Kitchen Barbarians” by Jason Kwon The Lehman desk had been dead for six years, but still haunted the 47th floor of One Bryant Park. Jack Kwon could feel it some nights: the residual hum of 10,000 trades that had pulsed through this building, before the world ate itself in 2008. A new firm had leased the space, gutted it, and rebuilt it in glass and that shade of corporate gray that whispered we are serious people who do serious things , but the building’s bones remembered. Jack stood at the head of the conference table, Calacatta marble, 40 feet, custom-built for the room. Twelve men in bespoke suits pretended they weren’t nervous. They were nervous. He could smell it under the cologne and the leather and the recycled air, the sharp, animal scent of people who had staked reputations and capital on a deal that was still unsigned. The Meridian-Lux real estate acquisition. $740 million. Fourteen months of due diligence, back-channel negotiations, regulatory gymnastics, and the kind of financial engineering that made God-fearing people lose their religion. Jack had quarterbacked the whole thing from the buy side. Built the models, created the business plan, stress tested the assumptions until they either held or cracked, and the ones that cracked he rebuilt stronger. He was 30 years old and this was the biggest deal his firm had ever closed. In 17 minutes, the partners from both sides would sign documents that would rearrange a small corner of the American industrial landscape, and it was Jack’s architecture. Every number. Every projection. Every carefully-constructed argument for why Meridian’s office platform was worth 3.2 times revenue and not a penny less. He adjusted his watch. A white-gold Patek Philippe, its cobalt dial luminous beneath the sapphire crystal. A gift to himself after his first seven-figure bonus. His father would have called it wasteful. Jack bought it for the opposite reason. He knew what a 60-grand quiet-flex watch communicated in a room full of men who measured each other by such things. Charles Weston, senior partner, stood next to his young protégé. Silver-haired, 62, three market crashes and two divorces behind him, and he considered all acceptable costs of doing business. Eight years earlier, Weston had met Jack on the other side of a deal. While everyone else had seen a young associate, Weston had seen something rarer: patience, precision, and the instinct to kill when the moment came. The deal closed, and a month later, Weston poached him from the competing firm. He had recognized in Jack the same thing he looked for in undervalued investments, something the market had failed to price correctly. “We ready?” Weston whispered to Jack, ignoring the other suits in the room. “We’re ready,” Jack replied softly. “Lux’s counsel is asking about the earn-out provision again. Section 4.7.” “They can ask. The language is airtight. I wrote it.” “They want flexibility on the 18-month trigger.” “They can want. The trigger stays. Eighteen months, performance benchmarks met, or the earn-out doesn’t vest. That’s not a negotiating position. Trust me, they’ll fold.” Weston studied him. The older partner had a way of looking at people that reminded Jack of a jeweler examining a stone: tilting it, testing it, deciding what it was worth. “You’re sure?” “I’m sure.” “Seven hundred and forty million dollars sure?” Jack met his eyes. “Feed me to the wolves if I’m wrong.” The conference room was silent except for the whisper of climate control and the muted pulse of Manhattan 47 stories below: taxis, sirens, the grinding machinery of a city that never stopped. The signing proceeded. Jack tracked the signatures, which belonged to the principals, the men whose names would appear on the documents and whose photographs would appear in The Wall Street Journal . Jack’s name would not appear anywhere, by design. Private equity deal guys were architects, not buildings. You constructed the thing and someone else’s name went on the door. Twelve signatures to execute the final agreement. The scratch of Mont Blanc pens on paper that smelled of fresh ink and old power. When the last signature was applied, the room exhaled around Jeff Rothschild, senior partner at Lux Capital, who rose first and buttoned his blazer. The rest of his team stood with him. Handshakes, the firm grip of men sealing something irrevocable. Smiles rooted in real pleasure, relief, the primal satisfaction of people who had just made each other rich. Weston caught Jack’s eye across the room and gave him the nod. You did this. We don’t need to say it out loud. Jack nodded back, then turned to his laptop and closed the deal model. Twenty-seven tabs of Excel, every assumption and projection he’d lived inside over the past four months. Beneath them was another browser tab he’d opened at 3:00 AM, before the final morning of negotiations, when the conference room was empty and the cleaning crew was running vacuums in the hall. A recipe. Canard à la Rouennaise, Rouen-style pressed duck, one of the most technically demanding dishes in classical French cuisine. The preparation required bleeding the duck by strangulation, rather than slitting its throat, to keep the blood in the meat, then roasting it rare, carving tableside, and pressing the carcass in a silver duck press to extract a sauce of blood and bone marrow and Cognac. In the opinion of every chef who had ever attempted it, this was either the pinnacle of culinary art or an act of beautiful insanity. Jack had been studying the recipe for weeks. Not casually, with YouTube videos and weekend attempts, but the way he studied deal structures. Obsessively. Completely. He’d found a 1927 Larousse Gastronomique entry that described the pressing technique in details that bordered on pornographic. He’d cross-referenced three different preparations—Escoffier’s, Ducasse’s modern interpretation, and a handwritten recipe from a retired chef at Tour d’Argent that he’d found in an obscure culinary archive online—and synthesized them into his own version: one investment thesis built from competing sources. He’d adjusted ratios mentally a dozen times before touching an ingredient, tasting each step in his imagination, feeling the sauce come together: the iron minerality of the blood, the warmth of the Cognac, the silk of the butter. He’d sourced a duck press from an antiques dealer in Connecticut: silver-plated, French, circa 1890, $800, the most irrational purchase he’d made since the Hermès tie, and the only one that made him feel anything. He closed the browser tab before anyone could see it. The recipe vanished, replaced by the Bloomberg screensaver, the scrolling green-and-white data of a financial world that never slept. They went to Per Se, Thomas Keller’s three-Michelin-star restaurant, the dinner theater of New York’s finest. Chef Keller was one of the most iconic chefs in American history. The group was 12 deep: deal team, partners, two Sullivan & Cromwell lawyers who charged $1,900 an hour to drink Barolo at someone else’s expense. “To Kwon,” Weston said, raising his glass. “The racehorse that doesn’t stop.” The table raised glasses, crystal catching candlelight. Jack raised his. Smiled. Drank. The bourbon was Pappy Van Winkle, 23-year. Three hundred and fifty dollars a pour. It tasted like oak and vanilla and caramel and the accumulated patience of nearly a quarter century in a barrel, and it was, objectively, one of the finest things a human being could put in their mouth. Jack experienced almost none of its joy. He registered the gentle tickle and the warmth and the familiar loosening behind his sternum, but the flavor, the thing that made a $350 pour worth $350, passed through him. items.title: Hollywood’s Tech-Founder Fixation Takes a Dark Turn
items.summary: Tech-entrepreneur bio-pics used to give us flawed men who built great products. But the latest wave of movies, from “The Social Reckoning” to “Artificial,” recast Silicon Valley titans as unambiguous villains, and suggest that the products themselves are the threat.
items.title_original: Hollywood’s Tech-Founder Fixation Takes a Dark Turn
items.title_en: Hollywood’s Tech-Founder Fixation Takes a Dark Turn
items.title_zh: 好莱坞对科技创始人的痴迷走向了阴暗面——科技企业家传记片曾向我们展现过那些虽有缺陷却创造了伟大产品的男性。但从《社交清算》到《人工智能》，最新一波电影将硅谷巨头们塑造成不折不扣的反派，并暗示产品本身才是威胁。

items.title: How a Canadian TV Show May Have Helped Foil the FlyDubai Terrorist Attack
items.summary: The documentary series “Air Crash Investigations” has attracted a cult following by obsessively dissecting historic plane crashes. Then a fan of the show found himself aboard a hijacked plane headed for Israel.
items.title_original: How a Canadian TV Show May Have Helped Foil the FlyDubai Terrorist Attack
items.title_en: How a Canadian TV Show May Have Helped Foil the FlyDubai Terrorist Attack
items.title_zh: 一部加拿大电视节目如何可能帮助挫败了“飞迪拜”恐怖袭击事件——纪录片系列《空难调查》因对历史上的空难事件进行深入剖析而吸引了一批忠实粉丝。随后，该节目的某位粉丝发现自己身处一架飞往以色列的遭劫持航班上。
